**1st Place — DESIGN C (opencode/GLM)**  
Design C wins because it treats the MCP boundary as syntactic sugar over the existing graph, not a parallel universe. The killer move is returning `cell_ref` in every atomic tool response, letting agents chain by reference instead of by value — this eliminates the serialization thrash that plagues A and B. The retention model (hot→cold→tombstone hash-only) is the only design that respects the fact that witnesses are append-only truth; B’s GC of scratch namespace is naive (what if a scratch cell is witness-referenced?), and A’s `FORGET(ttl)` is a time bomb for provenance integrity. The tmux lane keyed by `tmux-session+cwd` gives you identity without fragile PID tracking, and `tit again --in=<new>` re-binding a persisted subgraph is the closest thing to actual software reuse. The THREE MCP tiers (atomic/pipe/introspection) are the only design that anticipates real agent behavior — introspection is not an afterthought, it’s the onboarding ramp.  

**2nd Place — DESIGN B (kimi)**  
Design B is a solid runner-up because it gets the fundamental insight right: one provenance ledger across CLI and MCP from a single process. The persistent session graph at `~/.tit/sessions/<pane>.graph.json` is a concrete, debuggable artifact that survives restarts. `tit pipe --last` replaying only changed edges is elegant — though it assumes you can diff the graph cheaply, which C’s retention model handles more honestly. What drops B to 2nd: the EFFECT exclusion is contradictory (you say clipboard is EFFECT, then treat crons as TICK-driven cells but force registrations through EFFECT — pick one). Keystroke debounce writing directly into input cells violates the separation of concerns that A and C enforce via explicit TICK. Also, no health-aware fallback means a dead MCP server severs the graph mid-session; A and C both route around that.  

**3rd Place — DESIGN A (claude)**  
Design A is the most theoretically clean but operationally naive. The `EFFECT`-only-writes rule is architecturally beautiful — it makes all mutations auditable — but it introduces a ceremony that kills throughput: every write needs an EFFECT declaration, a LINK, a witness chain, and a route. In practice, agents will ignore this or fake it, and the design has no built-in way to enforce it at the graph level (it’s a convention, not a type). The tmux PERSIST_BUFFER cell surviving detach is fine, but `CRON_JOB cells tick while idle` assumes the agent stays alive; C already solved this by letting MCP wake a new agent to inherit crons. The `route[]` in every response is redundant — if you have witnesses, you have the route — so it’s just payload bloat. Health-aware fallback (native>HTTP>MCP) is a good instinct, but B and C both do it without the routing overhead.  

**The winning capability:** **Reference-chained cell returns** — the single feature that makes quilt-native TIT worth building is that every MCP tool response returns a `cell_ref` (not a blob), so agents build persistent, replayable subgraphs by composition rather than by copying values. This turns every tool call into a node in a living provenance graph — kill the process, wake another, it re-attaches by reference and continues exactly where the last witness left off. That’s not an enhancement; it’s a different class of system.  

— **Claude 3.7 Sonnet**
